articles.title: Rohit Sharma on the verge of multiple milestones! 21K international runs, 400 ODI sixes in sight against New Zealand
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Rohit Sharma will have more than just runs on his mind when India take on New Zealand in the upcoming five-match ODI series, starting in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Rohit Sharma will have more than just runs on his mind when India take on New Zealand in the upcoming five-match ODI series, starting in Auckland on Wednesday. The Indian opener is on the brink of several significant milestones and could add multiple records to his already impressive career during the series.The 'Hitman' heads into the New Zealand challenge on the back of a prolific run against West Indies at home, where he scored 225 runs in three innings at an average of 75, including a century and a half-century. He has also enjoyed a productive year in ODIs, accumulating 604 runs in 12 innings at an average of 50.33 and a strike rate of 104.67, with two centuries and two fifties.Rohit, who has scored 12,120 runs in 291 ODIs, will be looking to carry that form into the New Zealand series. Here are five major milestones he could achieve.21,000 international runs and 5,000 in SENA conditionsRohit is just 348 runs away from becoming the latest Indian batter to cross the 21,000-run mark in international cricket. He has accumulated 20,652 runs in 517 matches and 550 innings at an average of 42.66, including 52 centuries and 113 fifties.He is also closing in on another significant overseas milestone. With 4,964 international runs as an opener in SENA conditions, Rohit needs just 36 more to become the first Indian opening batter to reach 5,000 runs in South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia. His tally includes 17 centuries and 23 fifties in 114 matches.A century in New Zealand would also put him in an exclusive club. Rohit needs one ODI hundred in the country to become the fourth Indian batter, after Sachin Tendulkar, Virat Kohli and Shikhar Dhawan, to score ODI centuries in all four SENA nations.400 ODI sixes and 15,000 runs in winning causesRohit is already the leading six-hitter in ODI history, with 381 maximums to his name. He needs 19 more to become the first batter to smash 400 sixes in the format. He is also 26 sixes away from reaching 700 maximums in international cricket.Another landmark awaits him in winning causes. Rohit has scored 14,817 international runs in matches won by his teams and needs 183 more to reach 15,000. Only Ricky Ponting (20,140), Virat Kohli (18,589) and Sachin Tendulkar (17,113) have crossed that mark.Rohit looks to silence doubters ahead of 2027 World CupDespite continued discussions around his place and form ahead of the 2027 ODI World Cup, Rohit has remained among India's most productive batters in the format. His 35 centuries and 63 fifties underline his consistency, while his recent performances against West Indies offer further encouragement.In New Zealand, where he has scored 437 runs in 14 ODIs at an average of 36.41, including four half-centuries, Rohit will be aiming to make an impact while chasing some major personal milestones.The five-match series presents another opportunity for the veteran opener to add to his legacy and strengthen India's preparations for the next World Cup.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'The Big Show' is over: Glenn Maxwell announces retirement from international cricket
articles.summary: Australian all-rounder Glenn Maxwell has announced his retirement from international cricket, bringing an end to a career in which he entertained fans
articles.body: Australian all-rounder Glenn Maxwell has announced his retirement from international cricket, bringing an end to a career in which he entertained fans with his aggressive batting and unusual shots. Maxwell made the announcement on Tuesday during an episode of The Final Word podcast. His decision also includes his retirement from domestic 50-over and four-day cricket for Victoria.Maxwell, popularly known as 'The Big Show', represented Australia in 149 ODIs, 130 T20Is and seven Test matches. He was part of Australia's 2015 and 2023 ODI World Cup-winning teams and also played a key role in the team's T20 World Cup triumph in 2021."I'm going to be announcing my retirement from international cricket and domestic games for Victoria in the 50 over and the four-day stuff, red ball completely," the 38-year-old told The Final Word podcast in an episode released on Tuesday.Wants to focus on fitnessMaxwell said he wants to give more attention to his fitness and prepare his body for the remaining tournaments in his career."It's probably a time where I probably need to spend a little bit more time investing in the body to make sure I can get through the remaining couple of tournaments I've got in my career."He scored 3,990 runs in ODIs and 2,897 runs in T20 internationals. His last appearance for Australia came against Oman at the T20 World Cup in Sri Lanka in February.Maxwell also made a special mark in T20 cricket. Along with India's Rohit Sharma, he remains one of only two players to score five international centuries in the format.With his off-spin bowling, he also picked up 128 wickets for Australia in the two shorter formats.Misses chance for MCG farewellMaxwell had retired from ODI cricket last year but was hoping to play one final international match at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).However, that possibility ended when Australia announced its squad for the upcoming series against England on Monday. The selectors have focused on younger players in their short-format plans.Maxwell admitted that he had hoped to get a farewell match at his home ground but understood the team's decision."There was, I suppose, a small hope or discussion that I might have been able to potentially get a send-off game at the MCG, but I can completely understand the direction they're going with this squad," he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Rajat Paliwal's 21st first-class ton: A century without knowing he was nearing one
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ravikant has kept Palam's Air Force Complex Ground ticking for the past 35 years.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ravikant has kept Palam's Air Force Complex Ground ticking for the past 35 years. The chief ground staff member, he also doubles up as the scoreboard operator. But when cricket resumed after the COVID pandemic, he received an unusual request from the Services captain Rajat Paliwal: he did not want his name displayed on the scoreboard while batting.Ravikant, a little hesitant at first, agreed."Sab ka apna apna hota hai. Kaptaan sahab ka farman aaya aur humne maan liya (Everyone has their own superstition. He made the request and I accepted it)," Ravikant said.On Monday, the 34-year-old Paliwal smashed his 21st first-class century to rescue Services, who were reeling at 27 for three, and took them to 266 on the opening day of their Ranji Trophy Group C clash against Delhi. He remained unbeaten on 111 off 196 balls.With no name appearing against Batsman 2 (Paliwal) on the scoreboard, the veteran batter had no way of knowing how close he was to his century. He eventually realised he had reached the milestone through the reaction of Delhi's fielders, who began closing in around him."I got to know that I was getting closer to a century when I saw more fielders around me. I realised I had scored a hundred only through the reaction of the Delhi players," he told reporters at the end of the opening day."I started this practice sometime after Covid. Sometimes, I used to feel a little nervous and lose my focus. The scoreboard draws attention, so I have taken it out of the picture entirely to concentrate only on the game," he added.This was Paliwal's highest score of the season so far, and he described it as particularly special. When he walked out to bat, Services were staring at the possibility of being bowled out for less than 100. But Paliwal stood up for his team, as he has done for nearly a decade-and-a-half."This hundred is very special, especially because the team had lost four wickets for 44 runs and we needed this knock. This has come after a long time and at a critical juncture before a break, to set the tone for the next phase," he said.Yes, I look at Paras as an example. He has crossed 10,000 runs in first-class cricket and has been remarkably consistent. Last year, he also won the Ranji Trophy title. His persistence and consistency are inspiring.Paliwal, who turns 35 in December, knows that his chances of breaking into the Indian team are now limited. However, he continues to draw inspiration from Jammu and Kashmir captain Paras Dogra, 41, with whom he remains in regular touch."Yes, I look at Paras as an example. He has crossed 10,000 runs in first-class cricket and has been remarkably consistent. Last year, he also won the Ranji Trophy title. His persistence and consistency are inspiring. Paras has been an inspiration in this regard. He became a Ranji Trophy champion in his forties. When you see him consistently performing at that age, you feel confident about yourself as well," he said."Yashpal [Singh] is another player who has influenced me a lot. He scored a lot of runs and played alongside me for four or five years when I started. We had some very good partnerships together," he added.A bulwark of India's domestic cricket circuit, Paliwal believes that the love for first-class cricket in the country is far from fading. He cited his Delhi counterpart, Ayush Badoni, who has scored back-to-back double centuries, as an example of the continued appetite for the longer format."It's true that cricket has become much faster. Throughout the year, there is a lot of focus on T20 cricket because of the exposure, media coverage and attention it receives. But you cannot categorise players like that. If you look at Badoni, he has scored two double centuries on the trot. Badoni is my opponent, but I would like to appreciate him because it is not easy to score back-to-back double hundreds."Every player has individual priorities, and everyone approaches the game differently. Everyone has their own preferences and ambitions. Some want to establish themselves in this format, while others prefer the shorter formats. But I believe many players still try to perform in the longest format as well," he continued.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Top four is set': Shubman Gill reveals India's No. 5, No. 6 plans ahead of New Zealand ODIs
articles.summary: India captain Shubman Gill has outlined the team's plans for the middle order ahead of the five-match ODI series against New Zealand.
articles.body: India captain Shubman Gill has outlined the team's plans for the middle order ahead of the five-match ODI series against New Zealand. Gill said India will adopt a flexible approach for the No. 5 and No. 6 positions, with Axar Patel and KL Rahul expected to take up these roles depending on the match situation.India will begin the series against New Zealand on Wednesday at Eden Park in Auckland. According to Gill, the top four batting positions are settled, while the team is open to making changes in the middle order."We will have floating approach for no.5 and no.6. Our top four is set, all right-handers. So if lefty is needed, Axar bhai goes and depending on match situation even KL bhai can go. So bit flexible," Gill said ahead of the opening ODI match.Gill plays down concerns over neck issueGill also dismissed concerns about his neck, which had troubled him in the past.The India captain suffered a cervical disc bulge and neck spasm that affected his nerves in late 2025. The injury kept him out of international cricket for nearly a month.He had suffered the injury on the second day of the Kolkata Test against South Africa and was taken to hospital for examination after the day's play. He remained under observation and was discharged the following day before travelling to Guwahati on November 19, 2025.However, Gill said he was not experiencing any discomfort and had completed his batting and fielding duties without any problems."No issue… I batter for close to one and a half hours and did my fielding without any trouble too. articles.title: Blueprint under construction: India look to solve 2027 World Cup bowling puzzle in New Zealand ODI series
articles.summary: India have a fair idea of what their ideal ODI bowling attack should look like.
articles.body: India have a fair idea of what their ideal ODI bowling attack should look like. What remains uncertain is who, beyond the established names, will fill the remaining pieces of the puzzle.Jasprit Bumrah remains India's undisputed spearhead, while Mohammed Siraj is the closest thing to a settled second seamer. Beyond that, however, the pecking order is far from finalised. Arshdeep Singh's left-arm variety has made him a proven force in T20Is, but he is still relatively untested in the 50-over format. Gurnoor Brar is only beginning to find his feet, while India's search for a reliable pace-bowling all-rounder capable of easing the dependence on Hardik Pandya remains unresolved.That is why the five-match ODI series against New Zealand, beginning in Auckland on Wednesday, carries significance far beyond a routine bilateral contest. With the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa now less than a year away, India are running out of opportunities to answer some critical questions about their bowling resources.The absence of Bumrah and Pandya from the tour has already shifted greater responsibility onto a young attack. The blow was compounded by Prasidh Krishna's hamstring injury, ruling out a bowler widely viewed as a near-certain World Cup pick, especially given the fact that he is a tall, hit-the-deck bowler, the kind that does well on pitches in South Africa.Siraj, with 51 ODIs behind him, becomes the senior figure in the pace unit. Around him are bowlers rich in promise but short on experience. Arshdeep has played just 18 ODIs, Gurnoor only nine, while Auqib Nabi and Anshul Kamboj are still trying to establish themselves at the international level.Head coach Gautam Gambhir was unusually frank when he described the group as potentially India's "most inexperienced ODI bowling attack". His assessment also underscored the importance of the assignment. If India prosper in New Zealand, it will be because this attack has risen to the challenge in conditions not traditionally in India's comfort zone.Beyond evaluating individuals, India must identify specialists for every phase of an ODI innings: new-ball operators, middle-overs enforcers, bowlers who can bowl dry and death-bowling finishers. Equally important is finding combinations that can succeed in conditions similar to those expected in South Africa.And when one talks about weaknesses, the seam-bowling all-rounder question springs up. Nitish Kumar Reddy has emerged as a possible backup to Hardik and in the T20Is, one saw him bowl the difficult overs and bowl with increased pace and effectiveness, but with only eight ODIs and limited evidence of his effectiveness as a fifth bowling option, he remains a work in progress. He will also be featuring in only the first ODI as India are looking to play him in the Test matches.The batting unit, though, gives greater comfort and offers greater certainty. Questions around Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli's future have gradually given way to discussions on how best to maximise their experience. Shubman Gill, meanwhile, has an opportunity to strengthen his credentials as ODI captain, leading in the first three matches before Shreyas Iyer takes charge for the final two as Gill prepares for Tests.For India, this tour is less about immediate results and more about gaining much-needed clarity. The World Cup blueprint is taking shape. The bowlers now have five matches to prove they belong in it."If we do well in the One-day series, the credit will go to this bowling attack. It will go to these boys. When you come overseas, your bowlers win the series, especially in One-day and Test cricket," Gambhir stressed.India have three ODIs against Sri Lanka in Dec and another three against Zimbabwe in Jan. But those games are in Indian conditions which are vastly different from South Africa. If the team has to identify weaknesses and address them, it has to be here, in New Zealand.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Harsh on Jasprit Bumrah to say he’s picking and choosing matches': Shane Bond
articles.summary: With a packed international calendar forcing teams to constantly juggle workloads and preparation, both India and New Zealand have taken steps to keep
articles.body: With a packed international calendar forcing teams to constantly juggle workloads and preparation, both India and New Zealand have taken steps to keep their key bowlers fresh for the upcoming Test series that will conclude a tour stretching beyond 40 days. Several frontline players were released from the final two ODIs to focus on red-ball cricket, while India opted not to include Jasprit Bumrah in the ODI squad, allowing him to concentrate exclusively on the Tests.In an interview with TOI, former New Zealand pace great Shane Bond discussed the challenges of player management, the value of ODI cricket as Test preparation, and the recurring debate surrounding Bumrah’s availability.Excerpts:How challenging is it to navigate tight schedules, player availability and preparation?It’s a challenge. When I look back at my playing days, the best players in a country would generally play two formats, sometimes all three. The schedule was never as congested as it is now. If you were in the New Zealand team, you were among the best 11, 12 or 13 cricketers in the country. Today, you often see two Indian teams playing simultaneously. New Zealand, too, can field very different squads around the world depending on the schedule.Both teams have split squads for the ODI series. Is that the right approach when turnaround times are short?It’s simply part of modern cricket. Personally, I always enjoyed playing One-day cricket before a Test series because, as a bowler, you spent three-and-a-half hours on your feet and delivered 10 overs at high intensity. I felt it was ideal preparation because a two-hour Test session suddenly seemed relatively short. The only challenge was handling those extra overs.Does match time still trump net practice as preparation?Absolutely. Nothing replicates time spent on your feet in a match. You can do all the training and net sessions you want, but it doesn’t compare to standing in the field, running from fine leg to mid-on and maintaining that intensity for six hours.That’s the kind of preparation players need, not just bowling in the nets.Does it make sense for Jasprit Bumrah to skip the ODIs ahead of the Test series?There’s often a perception that players are simply picking and choosing what they want to play. I don’t think that’s the case at all. Experienced bowlers understand their bodies very well. They’re constantly discussing their workloads with medical staff and coaches, assessing what they can physically handle.The biggest risk period is always when a player is returning from injury and readjusting to competitive cricket. That’s why I think it’s pretty harsh on Booms (Bumrah) to suggest he’s picking and choosing.Does workload management become even more important with the ODI World Cup next year?It applies not just to Booms but to every player. India play an enormous amount of cricket, so managing workloads is essential. You want your best players fit, fresh and ready when the World Cup arrives next Oct or Nov. Every major cricket nation is trying to achieve the same balance, especially with the demands of both international and franchise cricket.Is that realistic given the packed Future Tours Programme?It’s extremely difficult. Australia, for example, are currently in South Africa before heading home, and then they have a four-Test series against New Zealand. They’re working hard to protect their fast bowlers. New Zealand, too, want their best pace attack available for that Australia tour.It’s a constant challenge for coaches, trainers and support staff around the world.What is your assessment of India’s current pace attack?I’m a huge fan of Mohammed Siraj. I love his energy and body language. He’s been performing consistently across formats for a long time. India have a very well-balanced attack. The one thing they perhaps lack is a left-arm fast bowler, but they’ve got height, pace and skill. They hit the seam hard and, importantly, they have depth.Even someone like Aquib Nabi has come through and looks a quality bowler. Akash Deep is a good bowler too. As a coach, Gautam Gambhir will want enough options to rest and rotate players, and India certainly have that luxury.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ranji Trophy: Rajat Paliwal's ton, Aman Chaudhary's 4/79 define Day 1
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Services captain Rajat Paliwal is about to turn 35. He draws inspiration from the persistence of J&K's 41-year-old captain Paras Dogra.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Services captain Rajat Paliwal is about to turn 35. He draws inspiration from the persistence of J&K's 41-year-old captain Paras Dogra. On Monday, he was up against Aman Chaudhary - a 21-year-old left-arm spinner - who emerged as Delhi's trump card in just his second first-class game.The word 'relentless' is tattooed on Chaudhary's arm; and on a slow-turning first-day track at the Air Force ground in Palam, Paliwal, with an unbeaten 111, threatened to take the game away from Delhi. But it was Chaudhary's probing spell of 4/79 (in 31 overs) that helped Delhi bowl out Services for 266 at stumps in their Ranji Trophy Elite Group C game.At the end of the day's play, Paliwal, who has 110 first-class matches behind him, didn't want to judge the new-age cricketers who unapologetically prioritise T20 cricket over first-class cricket. He cited Delhi captain Ayush Badoni's consecutive double centuries this season to validate the depth of Indian domestic cricket and then went on to talk about Dogra - Paliwal's "inspiration"."My inspiration is Paras Dogra. He got to lift the Ranji Trophy at this stage and age," Paliwal said, who, earlier in the day, managed to steer his team from a precarious 158/7 to a competitive total on a pitch that's likely to deteriorate.Harsh Dubey claims 9 wktsSpinner Harsh Dubey's sensational spell of nine for 53 headlined a dramatic opening day as 14 wickets fell in the Elite Group A Ranji Trophy clash between Madhya Pradesh and Vidarbha, with the hosts struggling at 56 for four after bowling out the visitors for 209. articles.title: 'Chapter is maybe closed': R Ashwin fears Bhuvneshwar Kumar's India career could be over
articles.summary: Ravichandran Ashwin feels Bhuvneshwar Kumar could find it difficult to return to the Indian team after his disappointing comeback in the T20I series
articles.body: Ravichandran Ashwin feels Bhuvneshwar Kumar could find it difficult to return to the Indian team after his disappointing comeback in the T20I series against New Zealand. The former India spinner believes the door may have closed for the experienced pacer and has backed Mohammed Shami to get another opportunity.Bhuvneshwar returned to India's T20I side after a gap of four years but failed to make a strong impression. The 36-year-old managed just one wicket in four matches and conceded 180 runs.Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ashwin said Bhuvneshwar's performances in the series were nowhere close to the form he showed in IPL 2026."Bhuvneshwar Kumar hasn't bowled that well; he didn't prove his form," Ashwin said."There was a night and day difference between his IPL form and here (New Zealand series). I think that chapter is maybe closed. It's very difficult. How will he come back?" he added.Bhuvneshwar fails to make an impactBhuvneshwar earned his India comeback after an impressive IPL 2026 season, where he picked up 28 wickets in 16 matches and was arguably the best bowler of the tournament.However, he struggled to carry that form into the New Zealand series. In the opening T20I, he went wicketless and conceded 49 runs in four overs at an economy rate of 12.25.He picked up his only wicket of the series in the second match, dismissing Daryl Mitchell for six. However, he gave away 50 runs in his four overs.The experienced pacer failed to take a wicket in the third T20I as well, conceding 40 runs. He missed the fourth match before returning for the series finale, where he again went wicketless and conceded 41 runs.Overall, he finished the series with one wicket and an economy rate of 11.50.Ashwin questions Bhuvneshwar's preparationAshwin felt the difference in Bhuvneshwar's bowling intensity and speed was a major concern. He also questioned whether the pacer had prepared well enough before the series."Leave performance, leave giving extra runs. It's not that. What was disappointing, I felt the way he bowls in the IPL - the intensity, his run-up speed was lower, and his bowling speed was also lower. That tells me maybe he didn't come in prime training form for this series," Ashwin pointed out.He also explained why selectors could find it difficult to give an experienced player another opportunity after such a performance."If that's the condition, the selectors will also think, 'Is this the way'? If you're a new kid or a young boy, you'll get ten chances. But you're an experienced guy coming back," he further said.Ashwin backs Shami for India returnAshwin believes Mohammed Shami could now have a stronger case for an India comeback than Bhuvneshwar.Shami has not played for India in more than a year and a half but has shown good rhythm while representing Bengal in the ongoing Ranji Trophy."Right now I'm thinking that the way Shami is coming in Ranji and bowling, he is in much better rhythm (than Bhuvneshwar)," Ashwin stated.India's next T20I assignment will be a three-match home series against Sri Lanka in December.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: IND A vs NZ A: Yashasvi Jaiswal, Yash Rathod hit centuries as India A vs New Zealand A 2nd unofficial Test ends in draw
articles.summary: Yashasvi Jaiswal and Yash Rathod scored centuries as India A played out a draw against New Zealand A in the second unofficial Test at the Hagley Oval in
articles.body: Yashasvi Jaiswal and Yash Rathod scored centuries as India A played out a draw against New Zealand A in the second unofficial Test at the Hagley Oval in Christchurch. The visitors finished their second innings at 282/2 on Day 4, building a lead of 204 runs before both teams decided to shake hands.Jaiswal remained unbeaten on 155 off 162 balls, while Rathod scored an unbeaten 100 off 122 deliveries. The two left-handers shared an unbeaten 247-run partnership for the third wicket to put India A in a strong position.India A were waiting for Rathod to complete his century before the match was called off. He reached the landmark with a couple off Rhys Mariu, prompting celebrations before players from both teams shook hands.The match also saw more than 90 minutes of play lost due to rain on the final day.Jaiswal, Rathod lead India A's fightbackIndia A began Day 4 at 32/0 after safely negotiating the final 11 overs on the previous evening. However, the visitors suffered two quick blows after play resumed.Jarrod McKay dismissed Sai Sudharsan for 11, while Brett Randell removed Devdutt Padikkal for a duck in the next over. India A were reduced to 35/2 and needed a strong partnership to recover.Jaiswal took charge and attacked the New Zealand A bowlers. He found boundaries regularly and brought up his century off just 119 balls. Rathod provided excellent support at the other end and gradually increased his scoring rate. The pair did not allow the bowlers to settle and added 247 runs without being separated.Jaiswal finished with 15 fours and five sixes, while Rathod struck nine boundaries in his unbeaten knock.Rathod's century was particularly satisfying after he failed to make a big contribution in the first innings. He had also scored 44 not out and 66 in the previous match.The third and final unoffical Test will be played on November 7 at the Bert Sutcliffe Oval in Lincoln.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Fielding accident at Eden Park: Devon Conway ruled out of 1st India ODI after collision with Matt Henry
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: New Zealand have suffered another injury setback ahead of their five-match ODI series against India.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: New Zealand have suffered another injury setback ahead of their five-match ODI series against India. Opener Devon Conway has been ruled out of the first match after suffering a concussion during a training session at Eden Park in Auckland on Tuesday.Conway was involved in a collision with fast bowler Matt Henry while both players were attempting to take a catch during practice. The two players received immediate medical attention."Devon Conway and Matt Henry collided while attempting a catch during the BLACKCAPS training today at Eden Park. Both players were immediately treated by medical staff on-site and received Head Injury Assessments," a NZC media release said.Conway was taken to the hospital for further checks, which confirmed a concussion. He will miss Wednesday's opening ODI against India."Conway was taken to A&E for further examination which confirmed a concussion that has ruled him out of the first ODI against India tomorrow. Both players will continue to be monitored and their involvement in the Hero VIDA ODI series against India, Powered by Ai+ Nova Smartphone will be updated in due course," it said.Conway is the latest addition to New Zealand's injury list. Senior batters Mark Chapman and Rachin Ravindra have already been ruled out of the ODI series.Chapman is undergoing rehabilitation for a hamstring injury, while Ravindra is yet to recover from a shoulder problem.India-New Zealand ODI series scheduleIndia and New Zealand will begin their ODI series at Eden Park in Auckland on November 4. articles.title: Ranji Trophy: Karnataka leave Assam in deep trouble after twin fifers
articles.summary: Assam found themselves on the backfoot within a day of their Ranji Trophy Elite Group B fourth-round clash against Karnataka at Barsapara Cricket Stadium
articles.body: Assam found themselves on the backfoot within a day of their Ranji Trophy Elite Group B fourth-round clash against Karnataka at Barsapara Cricket Stadium on Monday with the visitors already securing the first-innings lead.Bowled out for a modest 135 and then unable to make significant inroads with the ball, the hosts watched Karnataka surge to 180 for two at stumps to take a commanding 45-run first-innings lead and seize early control of the contest in Guwahati.The damage was done largely by Karnataka’s spin duo of Ritesh Bhatkal and Shikhar Shetty, who shared all 10 wickets between them. Off-spinner Bhatkal returned figures of 5/35, while left-arm spinner Shetty claimed 5/53 as Assam collapsed after showing brief signs of resistance.Opting to bat first, Assam’s innings never recovered from a poor start that saw Nibir Deka, Pradyun Saikia and the promoted Sumit Ghadigaonkar back in the pavilion with only 30 runs on the board.Sibsankar Roy (37 off 66) and captain Denish Das (26 off 72) attempted to stabilise the innings, but Karnataka tightened their grip once Bhatkal removed both batters in his successive overs. The hosts then suffered a dramatic collapse, losing seven wickets for 42 runs to be dismissed cheaply.Having put Assam under pressure, Karnataka openers ensured there was no way back for the hosts.Rohan Patil and Mayank Agarwal dominated the Assam attack during a 129-run opening stand that effectively erased the deficit and laid the foundation for a sizeable lead. Patil was the aggressor, striking a fluent 89 off 87 balls with 13 fours and a six. articles.body: The India-Pakistan clash at the 2027 ODI World Cup has received 8.4 million ticket requests, despite the match being scheduled at a venue that can accommodate only 34,000 spectators. The contest will be played at The Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg on October 10 and has emerged as the tournament's most sought-after fixture so far.According to the International Cricket Council (ICC), the match has received 8,397,294 requests through the ongoing ticket ballot. The demand far exceeds the stadium's capacity.The World Cup final, which will also be held at The Wanderers Stadium on November 21, has received 7,900,944 requests, or nearly 79 lakh, making it the second-most sought-after match so far.The response to the ticket ballot has been high across the tournament. The ICC has received more than 120 million requests from fans in 193 countries, with 2.8 million unique fans registering their interest in attending the competition.The 2027 ODI World Cup will be co-hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. The tournament opener on October 7 will be a repeat of the 2023 final, in which Australia beat India in Ahmedabad.India-Pakistan is among the most anticipated fixtures in cricket and one of the tournament's biggest revenue-generating matches. However, India have dominated their recent meetings, winning their last nine encounters. Pakistan's last victory over India came in the 2022 Asia Cup.India and Pakistan are in a group with Australia, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and a qualifier. The other group comprises England, South Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and another qualifier.The top three teams from each group, along with the best fourth-placed team, will advance to the Super 7 stage. The top four teams from that stage will qualify for the semi-finals.How the ticket ballot worksEntry into the ticket ballot is free, and fans do not have to make any payment when registering.Each person can submit one ballot entry per match and can enter the ballot for multiple matches across the tournament.The ballot does not work on a first-come, first-served basis. Fans can register at any point during the ballot window, and the time of registration will not affect their chances of getting tickets.If the number of requests for a match exceeds the available ticket allocation, successful applicants will be selected through a randomised ballot process.The ICC will communicate the outcome of both successful and unsuccessful applications through the email addresses provided by fans during registration.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Seahawks' running game struggles in 34-17 home loss to the Bears
articles.summary: SEATTLE (AP) — The Seattle Seahawks returned two key pieces in their backfield and had a new big name on the offensive line. It wasn’t enough to spark their...
articles.body:
SEATTLE (AP) — The Seattle Seahawks returned two key pieces in their backfield and had a new big name on the offensive line. It wasn't enough to spark their struggling running game in a 34-17 loss to the Chicago Bears on Monday night.

"We have to watch the film," tailback Zach Charbonnet said. "But we've got to get a lot better. And quick."

Charbonnet made the start in the backfield, making his first appearance since he tore his ACL last January. First-round rookie Jadarian Price saw his first action since Week 3 after dealing with a rib injury that put him on injured reserve, entering for a play on Seattle's second drive and getting his first carry on its third.

The duo ran behind a line that was without Charles Cross — who suffered an ankle injury in the fourth quarter of last week's win over the Chiefs — but added Quenton Nelson after picking the eight-time Pro Bowler up in a trade with Indianapolis on Tuesday.

But as a unit, the Seahawks couldn't get much going, finishing with 81 yards rushing. Price led the way with 29 yards on 10 carries, while Charbonnet added 23 on six. Excluding quarterback Sam Darnold's 20 rushing yards — 14 of which came on one scramble late in the fourth quarter — Seattle averaged 3.59 yards per carry.

The rough outing brings the Seahawks down to 109.6 rushing yards per game through eight weeks. And its effects went beyond just the rushing numbers; Seattle went 1 for 11 on third down thanks in large part to the fact that it averaged 10.3 yards to go, the fourth-most of any team this season.

"We've got to improve very quickly in the run game," guard Grey Zabel said. "Got to get back to running the ball, take the pressure off our quarterback and wide receivers and our play-caller. Got to be able to move the line of scrimmage."

Charbonnet took a handoff on the first play from scrimmage of the night 5 yards upfield, eliciting a roar from the crowd at Lumen Field for his return.

"It's just a blessing to get back on the field," he said.

But the Seahawks wouldn't have another rush by a tailback go that long until the third quarter, when George Holani went for 9 yards on a third-and-18 draw. By the end of the night, the crowd was booing the run game, specifically back-to-back handoffs to Price that combined to get 3 yards with the clock ticking under seven minutes and the hosts trailing by 10.

Nelson's arrival, combined with Cross' injury, moved pieces all along the line. With Nelson taking his normal spot at left guard — learning the Seattle playbook and acclimating to the offense in less than a week — Zabel flipped sides to right guard. Josh Jones subbed in at left tackle.

"I think there were flashes," Zabel said. "But at the end of the day, moving pieces or not, you've got to go out and perform and do the best you can. Today wasn't good enough."

articles.body: India leg-spinner Prema Rawat set a new record in the Senior Women's T20 Trophy, scoring the fastest half-century in women's T20 cricket. Representing Uttarakhand against Hyderabad in the Senior Women’s T20 Trophy Elite match at the MCA Cricket Stadium in Gahunje, Pune, on Monday, the 24-year-old reached her fifty in just 14 balls. She bettered the previous record of 15 deliveries, held by Pakistan captain Fatima Sana.Prema remained unbeaten on 50 off 14 balls, hitting six fours and four sixes at a strike rate of 357.14. Her innings helped Uttarakhand post 187 for two after opting to bat first. She was also named Player of the Match for her all-round performance.Fatima had set the previous record in May 2026, when she scored a 15-ball fifty against Zimbabwe in Karachi. The Pakistan captain had broken the previous women's T20 International record of 18 balls, jointly held by New Zealand's Sophie Devine, Australia's Phoebe Litchfield and India's Richa Ghosh.Fatima's knock had also equalled the overall women's T20 record previously held by Marie Kelly and Laura Harris. Prema has now brought that mark down to 14 balls. However, Fatima still holds the record for the fastest fifty in a women's T20 International match.Uttarakhand's innings also featured contributions from openers Raghvi Bist, who scored 72 off 50 balls, and Kareena, who made 44 off 34 deliveries.Hyderabad struggled in the chase and failed to build partnerships, finishing at 98 for eight in 20 overs. articles.title: Cutting the angles: India's key to fielding success in Auckland
articles.summary: AUCKLAND: The Eden Park outfield was buzzing with activity as soon as the Indian cricket team got down to business ahead of the first ODI of the
articles.body: AUCKLAND: The Eden Park outfield was buzzing with activity as soon as the Indian cricket team got down to business ahead of the first ODI of the five-match series against New Zealand. Divided into groups of four, the players ran between two equidistant cones placed across the ground and intercepted deliveries fired by fielding coach Subhadeep Ghosh and other members of the support staff.The plan was simple: players were asked to call clearly and loudly while approaching the ball, and whoever reached it first had to fire it back to the thrower. The drill lasted around 30 minutes, emphasising the importance of running in straight lines, even when approaching the ball from different angles. The idea was to help players familiarise themselves with the ground's dimensions, which differ from those they are accustomed to.That is where the challenge lies in Auckland. The floodlights are different, the dimensions could feel unfamiliar, and ground fielding could become tricky, with plenty of opportunities to take twos in the deeper pockets.Former India fielding coach R Sridhar, who was with the team during its last tour, says Auckland's dimensions are different and challenging, making the concept of "cutting the angles" particularly important."Cutting the angle means running in straight lines. Simple. You assess the speed of the ball and the dimensions, and then you run towards the ball in a straight line. Awareness, the ability to run and take off quickly—all these things are the challenges," Sridhar told TOI.Other factors, such as wind, cold conditions and the match start time, will also come into play. However, the team has travelled extensively and should be equipped to deal with these variables. Having had just one training session before taking the field on Wednesday, adapting quickly to Eden Park will be crucial.Fielding is one area where India would want to put its best foot forward in the upcoming series, particularly with "catching efficiency" becoming an increasingly important metric.While India's fielding standards are generally better in ODIs than in T20Is and Tests, the team no longer has the watertight look it once did. In the 18 ODIs played since the change of captaincy in the format, beginning with the tour of Australia last year, India have dropped 27 catches, recording a below-par catching efficiency of 77.5%.Kuldeep Yadav has dropped five catches in the 11 matches he has played, while KL Rahul is second on the unwanted list with four drops in 16 games. Interestingly, Rohit Sharma has taken the most catches among Indian players in those 18 matches, topping the list with 15 catches and just two drops.Eden Park will be the first stop on the tour, which will then move to windy Wellington and Seddon Park in Hamilton before the five-match ODI series culminates at the picturesque Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui."Each venue has its own set of challenges. There is wind in Wellington, and different dimensions in Auckland—where the country side is bigger—but Bay Oval should be fine. It is on the open side, but conditions will be fine for adjustment," Sridhar said.On addressing India's fielding lapses, Sridhar emphasised that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to preparation. He believes the experience within the ODI squad will help the players navigate the challenges."Each player will be different. Preparation volume depends on the player's mental state, what the player needs at that point, and what he has done before. So there is a lot of basis in volume. You just can't go blindly and say everybody has to do this volume. It doesn't work that way. In ODIs, there is a lot of experience. You have Rohit, Virat, Gill. All of them have played there before. I'm sure they will do well too," said Sridhar.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Michael Atherton says Australia could 'implode' before Ashes and urges England to 'keep pressure on' in white-ball series
articles.summary: After the Test-series defeat in South Africa started a bumper run of marquee games, for Australia, Sky Sports' Michael Atherton feels things could go "horribly wrong" for Baggy Greens; England can add to the misery as they tour Australia for three ODIs and five T20s from November 13
articles.body:
A No 3 batter in Marnus Labuschagne who has gone 49 innings without a Test century and looks certain to be axed ahead of the impending home series against New Zealand.

Batting issues besides that, too, with the team rolled for 99 and 111 during the recent 2-1 loss in South Africa that saw their opponents displace them at the top of the Test rankings.

Selectors in the firing line after persisting with Labuschagne and also recalling Nic Maddinson, who had not played a first-class game since March 2025 and went on to total just 56 runs in four knocks in South Africa, including a 33-ball duck, before he was jettisoned.

A generational, certainly, but aging bowling attack that must cram in that four-match assignment versus New Zealand around Christmas, five Tests in India and the day-night 150th anniversary Test at home to England in March prior to the away Ashes next summer.

Michael Atherton can envisage an "implosion" before Australia arrive in the UK, telling the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast : "You could see it going horribly wrong, couldn't you?"

Australia under the pump ahead of white-ball series

England's Test team is not perfect - it could do with a frontline spinner as an option, for starters - but Joe Root's men will surely be taking some encouragement from Australia's travails in the longest format, even if they are unlikely to admit that publicly.

Now they have a chance to "keep the pressure on", in Atherton's words, as they embark on a white-ball tour of the country, a trip that comprises three one-day internationals - the first of which is on Friday November 13 (3.30am UK) - and five T20 internationals.

Australia have opted to rest pace stalwarts Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins for all eight matches but a number of Test players could be involved in the ODIs, including Travis Head, Alex Carey, Cameron Green and Matt Renshaw.

Atherton added: "Although some of the big guns are not playing, it is a chance to keep some pressure on Australia now - pressure on their selectors after the decisions around Labuschagne and what have you, pressure on some of their big-name players and pressure on them to keep their results modest.

"The past players will start to go at them as they started to do, actually, after about day one of the Ashes in Perth last year, before England then let them off the hook."

One of those past players to have his say after the third-Test thrashing by South Africa was David Warner , who branded the capitulation with the bat in Cape Town as "terrible", "disgraceful" and "un-Australian" while analysing the wreckage for Fox Sports .

What would be very Australian is to come back fighting when people have written you off.

Before last winter's Ashes they were told by many that they were too old but then promptly schooled a juvenile-at-times England en route to a 4-1 win that retained the urn.

Three years ago at the 50-over World Cup in India they were spanked by the hosts and then South Africa in their first two matches, only to win their next nine and claim a sixth title.

The point is that however much disarray Australia may seem to be in, they must not be taken lightly. If you do that, you are likely to get wounded. But, right now, England will feel they have a great chance to leave some pre-Ashes scars on their rivals.

For all this talk of Australia "imploding", though, let's not forget that England did that in Perth at the start of 2025-26 Ashes when, with the first Test in the palm of their hand, they gifted wickets with brainless drives and ended up losing inside two days.

This white-ball tour starts at the same venue and if England can avoid a repeat, then perhaps it will be Australia who cannot recover.

Schedule for England's tour of Australia

ODIs 3.30am UK time, with T20s 8.15am UK time

Second ODI: Sunday November 15 (Adelaide)

Third ODI: Wednesday November 18 (Hobart)

First T20I: Saturday November 21 (Melbourne)

Second T20I: Tuesday November 24 (Carrara)

Third T20I: Friday November 27 (Brisbane)

Fourth T20I: Sunday November 29 (Sydney)

Fifth T20I: Wednesday December 2 (Canberra)

articles.title: 'They're still playing very well': Mitchell Santner wary of Rohit Sharma-Virat Kohli threat
articles.summary: New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner knows the challenge his bowlers will face when they come up against India's experienced batters Rohit Sharma and
articles.body: New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner knows the challenge his bowlers will face when they come up against India's experienced batters Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli in the five-match ODI series. The first ODI will be played at Eden Park in in Auckland on Wednesday. Rohit and Kohli are now focused only on the 50-over format, but Santner believes they remain dangerous opponents.Santner believes the two veterans are still in excellent form and said his team will need to bowl with discipline to contain them."They're getting on, but they're still playing very well. We saw it in the last series against the West Indies. I've seen it for a long time. I've seen Rohit in the IPL as well," Santner said at the pre-match press conference.The New Zealand captain said his team's bowling plans would depend on the conditions. His bowlers will have to be ready for pitches that offer help to fast bowlers as well as those that provide little assistance."When it's doing a bit, what does it look like? And then when it's flat, what does that look like as well?" he said.Rohit and Kohli expected to draw big crowdsSantner also spoke about the excitement surrounding Rohit and Kohli's presence in New Zealand. He expects the two Indian stars to attract large crowds during the ODI series."...I think it draws the crowds. We've had some really good crowds throughout the T20 series, and I expect they'll be the same with Rohit and Virat being here," he said.Santner revealed that New Zealand's bowling group had already discussed India's batting line-up and how to tackle the experienced Indian batters in home conditions."We've obviously sat down as a bowling group and discussed what that looks like, what their line-up looks like, how to operate in New Zealand, which I guess we know how to operate on these pitches," he said.He also explained how Rohit and Kohli could set the tone for India's innings with an attacking approach at the top of the order."Their role is to go pretty hard at the top and then set up a good score in the middle and let their power come in at the end," Santner said."Rohit, obviously, and Kohli have done it for a long time. Shubman's been outstanding as well for the last five years," he added.Santner says short-ball tactic may not work against RohitSantner also pointed out that Rohit has improved his ability to deal with short-pitched deliveries. He said bowlers can no longer expect to trouble the Indian opener by repeatedly bowling short."Teams have tried to go short at Rohit before, but he hits those for six now," he said.The New Zealand skipper believes his bowlers will need to maintain pressure over long periods and make adjustments according to the pitch and match situation."If the pitch offers more than the other night, can you do it for a long period of time and challenge the batter? And then if it's flat, how do we change? What does it look like? Subtle field changes," he said.Santner added that there were no major secrets to bowling in ODI cricket and that his team would have to focus on building pressure and taking wickets."But I think there's not too many secrets with ODI cricket with bowling. It's just building pressure and trying to get wickets through that way."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: From boy wonder to leader: Shubman Gill returns to the land of his firsts
articles.summary: AUCKLAND: New Zealand holds a special place for Shubman Gill. In 2018, he was part of the U-19 team that triumphed here.
articles.body: AUCKLAND: New Zealand holds a special place for Shubman Gill. In 2018, he was part of the U-19 team that triumphed here. A year later, he made his ODI debut also on these shores. Now seven years after those two memorable ‘firsts’ in his cricketing journey, the 27-year-old is set to lead the side. From the eventful night in Mount Maunganui with the U-19 team to receiving his ODI cap from MS Dhoni in Hamilton, New Zealand will always hold a special place. Remembering these two events still brings a smile to the Indian captain's face."We won the U19 World Cup here. I have very good memories. I made my international debut here in New Zealand. Whenever I come here, I feel very good," said Gill at the pre-series press conference.The stakes, however, are much higher now. He is no longer the prolific young batter from Punjab trying to establish himself in international cricket. Now, he’s the man at the helm as India sharpen their preparations for the 2027 ODI World Cup. In 11 months, the team will compete for the ultimate prize in the 50-over format. The fixtures leading up to the tournament — beginning with the New Zealand series — offer the skipper an opportunity to find the answers India needs."I think the more we play at different venues, the more experience we get, and that will help us in the World Cup. From the T20 series, we have seen that there has been good bounce here with the new ball, which has challenged both the bowling and batting teams. So, both teams will face good challenges, and it will be a good challenge for us too. It is a young bowling attack, but we have all the qualities to succeed here. Hopefully, we will learn and do well," Gill said.While India's inexperienced bowling attack faces a significant test, the batting line-up looks formidable and settled. Not much has changed in the team's batting composition since the 2023 World Cup, and stability is expected to remain a key feature over the next 11 months."For us, No. 5 and No. 6 are a bit flexible. Our top four are pretty much set, and we are all right-handed batters there. If we feel we need a left-hander at No. 5, we can use Axar bhai. Or, if we feel the platform has been set for KL bhai to go out and play, we will decide according to the situation at that given point. The number of overs remaining and the position we are in matter more than fixed No. 5 and No. 6 positions.Injury-prone Hardik Pandya remains the crucial missing piece. However, even in his absence, the consistency of the established top four — Gill, Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer — leaves the captain with only the No. 5 and No. 6 positions to figure out. The decision, though, is less about personnel and more about the demands of a particular match situation."We are definitely very happy with our top order and middle order. If Hardik bhai comes in, then our No. 7 and No. 8 positions are also sorted, and we look like a much more balanced team in terms of our batting," Gill explained.Gill echoed head coach Gautam Gambhir's sentiments about the challenges posed by an inexperienced bowling attack, particularly in the absence of Jasprit Bumrah, Pandya and Prasidh Krishna. However, he sees the situation as an opportunity for the younger players to grow in confidence. Gurnoor Brar, Auqib Nabi, Anshul Kamboj and Arshdeep Singh, along with Nitish Kumar Reddy (for the first ODI only), are India's options. Gill believes the squad has the ability to "defeat any team in any condition.”"I feel that any Indian team that steps onto the ground is capable of defeating any team. Young players will gain a lot of confidence if they perform here. We will also gain confidence that if, for any reason, we don't have the team we want for the World Cup, our squad can still defeat any team in any condition. In that context, if we win the series here, it will be a big confidence booster for us," Gill said.Even as he plans for the series and next year's World Cup, Gill has ensured that the bigger picture does not distract him from his batting or his preparation for each fixture. The Indian captain arrived in Auckland well ahead of the series, accompanied by Brar, to begin preparations for the long tour. The focus now shifts to translating those hours in the nets into performances in the middle.The flashy youngster of 2018, with conspicuous streaks of colour in his hair, now carries the expectations of more than a billion people on his shoulders. The boy-wonder-turned-leader is focused on adding another memorable chapter to his New Zealand story."Hopefully, when we go back after a month, we will take a lot more good memories from here."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Process, routine, discipline': After scoring unbeaten 155 in unofficial Test, Yashasvi Jaiswal shares mantra of success in 'very cold' New Zealand
articles.summary: After a brief dip in form, young India batter Yashasvi Jaiswal has returned to scoring runs, with an unbeaten 155 for India A in the drawn second
articles.body: After a brief dip in form, young India batter Yashasvi Jaiswal has returned to scoring runs, with an unbeaten 155 for India A in the drawn second unofficial Test against New Zealand A in Christchurch on Tuesday. Jaiswal said he relies on "process, routine and discipline" to produce consistent performances.Jaiswal said the cold conditions in New Zealand made batting difficult, particularly early in the innings when the ball moved and the seamers found assistance."It's very cold here. The ball moves a lot initially and there is a lot of seam movement. And there are good bowlers hitting good areas consistently. So we have to wait a lot to make runs initially," he said.He added that batting became easier once the ball got older or the pitch settled, allowing him to play his shots."After that, when the wicket gets better or the ball gets old, it's easy to make runs. I won't say it's easy, but you can play good shots. So it was a lot of fun and it feels good to play here. It's a very different experience," he added.The century comes ahead of India's two-Test series against New Zealand, which begins on November 19. Jaiswal said discipline and sticking to his routine were key to handling the conditions."It's not that easy...Just focus on process, routine, discipline. I think you have to be very disciplined here," he explained.Speaking about the challenges of touring New Zealand, Jaiswal said the cold weather was the biggest difference compared to other countries he has played in."New Zealand is a very different place (compared) to India, Australia, even England. Because it's very cold here. If you look at the air, the whole day it was cloudy. Then for some time, the sun came and left. It's been like this for the last four days," he said.Asked how he adjusts his technique to suit the conditions, Jaiswal said he prefers to play close to his body and move towards the ball."Mainly, in my mind, the closer I play to the body, the better it is. Go to the ball and play. If you look at the first innings, my initial stance was behind. Then I changed again. If the bowler is not bowling fast, then you can manage the seam movement."If I get a loose ball, I will try to score runs. Rest is just an effort," he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: No time to catch their breath: Mitchell Santner flags New Zealand's recovery concerns ahead of first ODI
articles.summary: New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner said on Tuesday that his players were feeling \"a little jarred\" ahead of the ODI series against India after a packed
articles.body: New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner said on Tuesday that his players were feeling "a little jarred" ahead of the ODI series against India after a packed schedule that has seen the two teams play across all three formats in a little over a month.India and New Zealand are currently involved in a series comprising five T20Is, five ODIs and two Tests. The hosts lost the T20I series 2-3, with the first ODI scheduled to begin on Wednesday. The 50-over matches will also help New Zealand prepare for the 2027 World Cup, while the two-Test series, starting November 19, will be important for their chances of qualifying for the World Test Championship final.The T20I series was played across four venues and ended on November 1. India played their first match within 48 hours of arriving in Auckland, leaving little time for recovery after travel."It's a very quick turnaround. With the travel and the late finishes in T20 cricket, the guys are a little bit jarred today. Recovery is a massive part of the schedule at the moment," Santner said ahead of the first ODI.The New Zealand captain said the short gaps between matches made it difficult to field the same team throughout the series, even though teams would prefer to play their strongest available XI."With one-day cricket and quick turnarounds, it can be quite taxing. You want to play your best team all the time, but with the schedules these days and the quick turnarounds, it's pretty hard to do," he added.With the 2027 World Cup less than a year away, Santner also spoke about the possibility that it could be the last ODI tournament for several members of New Zealand's ageing squad, including him. The 34-year-old said the focus could shift towards T20 cricket after the tournament."Everyone's kind of 34 or 35. With one-day cricket being in the cycle, after this World Cup, the focus is going to shift again to T20 cricket, with the T20 World Cup being the next priority as well. So, yeah, I guess no one's told me anything yet, but it could be," said the 34-year-old.Santner said rotating players would be important during the series, particularly as New Zealand look to manage workloads across formats. He also pointed to the need to build depth by giving opportunities to other players."...it creates depth, and we've seen guys coming in and stepping up straight away," he said.He added that late finishes and dew during the T20I series had made recovery more important. With the ODIs scheduled to begin at 3pm local time, he expects dew to remain a factor towards the end of the second innings."With the dew, especially in the T20s, it was quite prominent, particularly in the second innings. With a 3pm (local time) start, it's probably going to be no different towards the back end of the second innings here around the country," he said.Santner said players would have to manage their recovery based on their individual needs, with training sessions sometimes giving way to rest."Guys just have to be on top of it. Whatever it looks like...So training might look like another recovery day rather than bowling a lot."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Past players will start to go at them': Ex-England cricketer warns Australia ahead of 2027 Ashes
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former England cricketer Michael Atherton believes England have a good opportunity to put Australia under pressure during their upcoming
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former England cricketer Michael Atherton believes England have a good opportunity to put Australia under pressure during their upcoming white-ball tour Down Under.He feels Australia's recent struggles, selection concerns and demanding international schedule could create bigger problems for the team ahead of the 2027 Ashes, potentially causing them to "implode".Australia recently suffered a 2-1 Test series defeat against South Africa, losing their position as the world's top-ranked Test team as well as their place at the top of the World Test Championship standings. Marnus Labuschagne's poor form has also raised questions about his place in the side.England will play three ODIs and five T20Is against Australia, with the ODI series beginning on November 13. The hosts will be without their experienced fast-bowling trio of Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, who are being managed ahead of a busy Test schedule. Australia are due to face New Zealand in a four-match Test series before travelling to India for five Tests in early 2027.Atherton wants England to keep Australia under pressureAtherton believes England should take advantage of Australia's current difficulties and make sure they do not get an easy run during the white-ball series."Although some of the big guns are not playing, it is a chance to keep some pressure on Australia now - pressure on their selectors after the decisions around Labuschagne and what have you, pressure on some of their big-name players and pressure on them to keep their results modest," Atherton said as quoted by Sky Sports.He also feels Australia's former players could become increasingly critical if the team continues to struggle."The past players will start to go at them as they started to do, actually, after about day one of the Ashes in Perth last year, before England then let them off the hook," he added.David Warner slams Australia's batting performanceAustralia's batting problems have also attracted criticism from former opener David Warner. The hosts were bowled out for just 111 in their second innings of the third Test against South Africa, losing the match by 176 runs and the series 2-1.Warner was particularly disappointed with the lack of fight shown by the batters."I'm just upset. It's terrible. It's un-Australian. There's no fight whatsoever. It's disgraceful," Warner said on Fox Sports. "288, you're winning a Test match; you could win a series. It's on the line. And this is the way they're playing?"He further criticised the batting unit for repeatedly failing to support the bowlers throughout the series."I think it's deplorable. The batters have let the bowlers down the whole series. Yes, Matt Renshaw showed fight in that first Test, but I think the batters have been disgraceful. What the batters should know is that this bloke here (Rabada) is going to come out firing. And he has done that. If you get through 10-15 overs..." Warner added.With the 2027 Ashes scheduled to begin in June, Australia will need to address these concerns before heading to England.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Ranji Trophy: Shams Mulani, Akash Anand rescue Mumbai with crucial half-centuries against Railways
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Shams Mulani and Akash Anand have been involved in many rescue acts for Mumbai.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Shams Mulani and Akash Anand have been involved in many rescue acts for Mumbai. On Tuesday, they once again came to the team's aid, scoring crucial half-centuries to help Mumbai post 396 on Day Two of their Group D clash against Railways at the Brabourne Stadium.At stumps, Railways were 116/2 in 35 overs, still trailing Mumbai by 280 runs.Resuming at 247/6, Mumbai needed their lower order to bat as long as possible on a wicket that was slowing down under the searing sun. Mulani and Anand did just that, putting their heads down, keeping the scoreboard ticking and stitching together an 82-run partnership off 150 balls for the seventh wicket. Against the run of play, Anand was trapped leg-before by Himanshu Sangwan (4/88). The wicketkeeper-batter scored 52 off 71 balls, with seven fours, registering the third half-century of his first-class career.It was the second crucial partnership Anand has been involved in this season. The first was a 210-run fifth-wicket stand with Sarfaraz Khan against Himachal Pradesh, which came off 344 balls. Anand had gone on to score an unbeaten 117 in that match.Mulani, who made 71 off 153 balls with seven fours, continued to forge small but valuable partnerships down the order to stretch Mumbai's total. He first added 35 runs off 56 balls for the eighth wicket with Tanush Kotian (20, 30b; 1x4, 1x6) and then 29 off 47 balls for the final wicket with Mohit Avasthi (15*, 21b; 1x4, 1x6) before becoming the last batter to be dismissed.Mulani said after the day's play that it was crucial for him and Anand to spend time in the middle. "The wicket got a bit slower and it wasn't swinging much because the conditions were sunny. But we negotiated the important first half-hour well and then capitalised on the loose balls. It put pressure on them, they spread the field, and we could easily rotate the strike," said Mulani, who brought up his 23rd first-class half-century.By the time Railways walked out to bat an hour before tea, the wicket had slowed down and was easier to bat on than it had been at the same stage on the opening day under overcast conditions, when Mumbai skipper Siddhesh Lad and Sarfaraz Khan were busy pulling out Mumbai from a hole they were in.With not much help, Mumbai's bowlers ensured they operated in the right channels and to the field, preventing Railways from scoring quickly. Railways got off to a solid start through openers Vivek Singh (38, 50b; 8x4) and Sahab Singh (33, 76b; 4x4), reaching 62 in 17 overs before Vivek retired hurt after being struck by a delivery from Avasthi.That provided the opening Mumbai were looking for and, within the next 10 overs, they removed two more Railways batters. Tanush Kotian (1/12) had Sahab caught behind in his second over of the innings, and seven balls later Mulani (1/29) deceived Eshaan Goyal, who chipped a catch straight to Siddhesh Lad at cover.Tushar Deshpande, who bowled with venom throughout the day, could have had Railways captain Bhargav Merai off a bouncer, but Musheer Khan lost sight of the ball in the sun at fine leg and, by the time he picked up its trajectory, it had bounced in front of him.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
